So, like, the white female secretary meeting her boss at the office and then getting married, and that helps with upward mobility.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And this is actually something I’ve been thinking about, because there’s some paper I read a while back about assortative mating, which basically means people matching on like to like rather than like versus unlike. And so what you’re seeing with the invention of the smartphone, with the invention of dating apps, etc., is that people are more able to sort for people who are like them. And so you’re actually seeing an increase in inequality, because rich people are marrying rich people instead of rich people kind of quasi-randomly running into, like, middle class or working class people and marrying them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And so, this sort of, like, relationship where, you know, a guy in the office — sort of, like, </span><em><span>Mad Men</span></em><span>-esque, like, you know — what’s his name, the guy with the — Roger? White-hair guy in </span><em><span>Mad Men</span></em><span>?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Roger Sterling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Roger Sterling marries — what’s her name? I forget the — the…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>I didn’t actually see the show. I just know that his character is Roger Sterling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>OK. Roger Sterling marries some brunette secretary in his office who comes to the office for the explicit purpose of, like, finding a guy. Like, many of the secretaries end up marrying or dating other men in the office. And what’s interesting is, in contemporary world — I mean, obviously that’s considered wrong for various reasons — but also, like, the impact of kind of meeting people in these algorithmic ways, especially in ways where you can sort on “Did you go to college? Where did you go to college? Do you have a postgraduate degree?” You can sort on these things that you have, like, like versus like.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And this is actually something that was, like, unexpected for me. I thought that dating apps would increase the level of meeting people that were different from you. And then I met my husband, where I was like, “You know, yeah, we’re super different.” I mean, he’s Jewish and he’s a single — he’s an only child. I was like, “Cool, we’re very different.” Then I found out that we grew up, like, I don’t know, a couple miles away from each other and attended the same school at different times. So I was just like, “Oh shit, how different are we really?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Yeah. One of my favorite — there’s a great chart here showing typewriter exposure and husband’s expected income.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Yeah.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Showing a really neat…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>We should show it on the screen.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>…kind of linear relationship there. I guess just, both to relate it to our prior book club episode about </span><em><span>The Feminine Mystique</span></em><span>…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Yeah.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>…I felt that Betty Friedan was a little downplaying of, like, material and technological changes in shaping social outcomes. This paper is definitely, you know, looking through the other end of the telescope on that, right?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The claim here is that the invention of mechanical typewriters generated this turn-of-the-20th-century boom in female employment. She is now looking back sort of nostalgically on that era as this, like, heyday that she wants to go back to — something like that. But, you know, there’s more than just ideas and takes happening here driving things.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, to the point about Jane Jacobs, it’s, like, it’s important to, you know — this paper, like most good empirical economics papers, has these, like, really annoying discussions where they’re trying to explain why they think this is a causal relationship and not just a correlation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Mm-hmm.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>As is often the case with these papers, I’m not as convinced as the actual authors of the paper that they have gotten this 100% right. That’s the yin and yang of life. People trying to get their paper published are like, “I’ve done the causal identification correctly.” The rest of us are looking at it like, “Eh, life’s always more complicated than that.” But they are trying.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Yeah.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>You know, there’s, like, a real good faith effort. It’s not just, you know, guy pointing at the screen being like, “Typewriters — a lot of ladies typing, a lot of ladies typing.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And Jacobs’ book — which is not just on her, it’s totally — I have learned, as we’ve gone through the great works of mid-20th century takes literature, she’s, like, making no effort at all to do this kind of causal identification work, right? She’s just, like — you could be saying that women are causing typewriters, that falling marriage rates are causing typewriter adoption. I think you actually hear a lot of contemporary conservatives doing this, right? They’re obsessed with email jobs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Yeah.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>And they think that liberals have invented email jobs in order to employ the girlbosses who we’re trying to keep away from their vocation as wives and mothers. And, you know, this paper is just reminding us that versions of this have been occurring in different ways all throughout time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s pretty clear that, like, 1880s leftists did not invent typewriter jobs in order to get women out of the home. And to create — you know, today it’s, like, illegal immigrants; at this time, it was African Americans doing the domestic work. But, like, no — like, technology happens.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like, these email jobs happen for a reason. The typewriter jobs happen for a reason. Technological change — you don’t need to like everything that’s downstream of it, although in this case it seems mostly benign. But, you know, just, like, shit happens, the world changes, and you gotta deal with it — including in its built environment and its impact on gender roles.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>I do think, too, that one thing that I think is said even now in contemporary discourse is that it’s bad to talk about household tasks as labor — that, like, doing the work of making your family food or cleaning up after your family, this sort of thing, is not, like, labor in the same sense. And it’s not treated as labor in, like, an economic sense. It is not — it’s, like, unpriced work that people are doing in the home.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But I think what this paper, like, often actually illustrates quite well is that, like, clearly people do think this is, like — and, like, it’s, like — in a world where, like, you yourself can’t do it, like, you will hire someone else to do it. And I actually really like this paper as a proof point for why we should treat that as uncompensated work that mostly women are doing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Yeah, well, but I think you’re misconstruing what the invisible labor is even.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>What do you mean?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Well, it’s not just the — I’m going to be the…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>You’re going to be woke for us?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Be there… yeah, it’s not just the literal performing of the household tasks, right? It’s the project management aspect. Somebody has to be the one who remembers, even if you have help, and so it’s just, like, who remembers what everybody’s schedule is. You know, in case people…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Yeah, that’s just another — I didn’t say invisible labor. That’s a different — you’re just…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Oh, OK.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Why are you mansplaining household labor to me?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>I don’t know. I don’t know. I don’t know why I am.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>You saw an opportunity to outwoke me and you took it. And then look where we are now.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>I’ve been seizing the day. I’ve been doing some solo parenting this week, and it’s — there’s a lot.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>And now you’re all in on invisible labor.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>There’s a lot going on. Yeah, there’s a large invisible emotional burden that is taking place. And I acknowledge that. I hear you. I see you, everybody who’s out there. And it’s challenging to outsource, because, you know, it just sort of inherently has to be done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Someday, I guess, AI will take care of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>I’m gonna be honest with you — as someone without children, you can throw this in my face one day — but I feel like you could outsource a lot of this stuff.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>All right, let’s record that one for posterity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>All right, guys, thanks for joining us. We haven’t picked our next book yet, so if you have thoughts on what book we should read, then you should definitely shoot it our way — either on Twitter, on email. But definitely subscribe, tell your friends about the podcast. We’re still growing, and we’ll see you next week.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><strong>Transcript</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yesterday, Donald Trump ordered Scott Bessent, the Secretary of theTreasury, to cut off all trade with Spain. Bessent said “Yes, sir.” Trump also said that this is because the Spaniards had stolen his strawberries. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Okay, I made up that second part, but he did in fact order Bessent to cut off all trade. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is not going to happen.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Presidents have a lot of discretionary authority on tariffs and trade, more than they should, but you do not have the right as president to impose tariffs on a country just because you don’t like their defense spending or you think that they haven’t been nice enough to you.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So this would not fly even in the Trump administration. Even with a supine congress and a permissive Supreme Court this is not going to happen. Also Spain is part of the European Union. So this is like Europe declaring “we’re cutting off all trade with Florida”: they can’t do that. And also, there’s a lot of U.S. business with Spain. In fact, Spain is one of those countries with which we run a trade surplus. So U.S. business would be howling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So this is all a non-event, this is is not something that is real. Except that the President of the United States did say this. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was completely crazy, and that’s the story that we should be taking from this. It’s not really at this point about economics. It doesn’t even make sense to talk about Trump Administration policies, let alone ideology. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What we have is President Sundowner. I mean, this this is completely insane stuff. In any kind of normally functioning political system, in any kind of normally functioning party environment we would have a massive bipartisan call across the aisle, across almost everybody except for a handful of members of congress who are themselves crazy, to say okay this guy is non compos mentis. We cannot leave the fate of the United States or the world in the hands of somebody who is completely irrational, who is making demands and believing himself to have powers that he does not. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And of course, instead, not only does everybody pretend that he’s still a rational human being, but the Republican Party, the Trump administration, is full-on engaged in trying to build a personality cult.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What this says to me is that the problem is a lot bigger than Trump. Something is fundamentally wrong with America, and at this point you don’t have to go through complicated justifications. You can just say something is wrong with a country and a system that lets this guy remain in a position of power.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Have a good day.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/98c24055-8d20-4d30-9a9e-63f844b97b24?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Wall Street Journal</a><span> describes a tense meeting among European leaders early this year, convened after Donald Trump threatened to use military force to seize Greenland from Denmark. According to the </span><em><span>Journal</span></em><span>,</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>heads of government were venting so emotionally about the 47th president that some of the nearly 30 leaders present would later call the session “therapy night.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yesterday, soon after he arrived in Ankara for the NATO Summit, Trump reiterated his demand that Denmark hand him </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d191d648-5f8d-48e9-ad20-5e645d256221?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">control of Greenland</a><span>.</span><span> But reactions were subdued. As far as I can tell, our erstwhile allies are now treating Trump as the senile uncle who says crazy, outrageous things, but shouldn’t be taken seriously.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What has changed? According to the </span><em><span>Journal</span></em><span>, European leaders have largely given up on hopes that they can bring back the America they used to know, and are quietly, in effect, declaring independence:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>American allies have begun pushing the gas pedal on an unprecedented experiment in de-Americanization. Authorities from France to the Netherlands are quietly removing American tech from their systems, adopting European open-source software and urging civil servants to no longer use Microsoft Teams or Office. Belatedly, they are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to try to boost Europe’s own private space firms, AI companies, and data centers, to avoid leaning on U.S. juggernauts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Europeans are running studies on where they would store their data or process their payments should friction with the U.S. escalate, and how well their American-made weaponry would operate without Washington’s authorization. Nations whose empires once spanned the globe are now stuck trying to extricate themselves from their humbling dependency on American technology and military power, without provoking the U.S.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Their willingness to de-Americanize partly reflects recognition that reconciliation is hopeless: Trump is who he is, and a nation that elected him twice simply can’t be trusted.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, Europe’s turn away from Trump also reflects plummeting perceptions of his power. At one time t</span><span>he world </span><span>feared Trump although it </span><span>never respected </span><span>him. The silence that met his renewed demand for Greenland shows that the world no longer takes him seriously.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>America </span><span>remains </span><span>an economic superpower with an enormous military budget. And the combination of a supine Republican Party</span><span>, along with</span><span> a </span><span>Supreme Court that </span><span>shamelessly </span><span>greenlights Trump’s authoritarianism, has given this president more control over</span><span> U.S. policy than any president has ever had, or ever should have. But </span><span>while Trump is able to run roughshod over Americans, he can no longer bully the rest of the world. Thanks to Trump, </span><span>the U.S. </span><span>has seen its global influence plunge.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are three big reasons for that precipitous decline.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, there is the debacle in Iran. Not only did Trump’s war of choice fail in all its objectives, it revealed that U.S. military power is far more limited than almost anyone realized. The insistence by Trump and his lackeys that this humiliating defeat was a great victory </span><span>shows that American foreign policy only serves to pander to Trump’s fragile ego. And when his ego meets reality, it slithers away.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In addition to showing the limits of U.S. military power, the war also showed the limits of U.S. financial power: It is increasingly easy for nations to bypass U.S. banks and the dollar using cryptocurrency — and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/550255d6-0a41-4aed-97a3-fb4cca92bb41?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Chinese yuan</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A second, in its way equally important, blow to U.S. prestige and influence has been Trump’s failure to deliver Ukraine to Vladimir Putin.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For make no mistake: everyone at that summit in Ankara knows that Trump, JD Vance and company both expected and hoped that their betrayal of Ukraine would lead to Russian victory. Surely, they imagined, Ukraine would be unable to hold off the onslaught from its much bigger neighbor without U.S. aid</span><span>. To America’s everlasting shame, </span><span>Trump told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that he didn’t “have the cards.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yet after Trump </span><span>cut U.S. aid to Ukraine by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b46fd008-e8a7-4a67-81a7-f9fef75d5658?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">99 percent</a><span>, Ukraine not only survived</span><span> but</span><span> began gaining the upper hand. Europe has stepped up financially, more or less replacing the lost American dollars. And Ukrainian military innovation has largely made up for the loss of American weapons.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The result has been to make </span><span>the U.S. increasingly</span><span> irrelevant. Put it this way: Iran taught foreign governments not to fear American might; </span><span>China, along with the crypto industry, has taught rogue countries that they needn’t fear American financial control; and</span><span> Ukraine has taught foreign governments that they don’t need American support</span><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Finally, Trump’s global power play rested on economics even more than on military force, above all on his belief that other nations would cower in fear at the prospect of facing U.S. tariffs. But Trump’s attempt to weaponize international trade has been a bust. Most notably, China’s economy has powered right through the Trump tariffs. Furthermore, it turns out that China has escalation dominance in the trade war: we need their rare earths more than they need access to our consumers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And other nations — even Canada and Mexico, which have historically been highly dependent on the U.S. market — are moving to reduce their dependence. Canada’s move to build a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fef0073e-355f-4107-83d0-ff937f507772?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">new pipeline</a><span> that will let it sell Alberta oil to Asia rather than the Midwest is just a highly visible symbol of a general world move toward bypassing America now that we have become an unstable, unreliable economic partner.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The combined effect of these humiliations for Trump and his minions has been a drastic reordering of America’s place in the world. For most of last year foreign leaders kept trying, desperately, to appease Trump. These days they’re mostly just humoring him, building a world in which his sundowning won’t matter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s extremely unlikely that anything substantive will come out of this NATO meeting. And a year ago the prospect of a failed summit would have been a source of deep concern. Now it will be met with a shrug: Nobody expects anything but chaotic bluster from Trump, and what he does matters less and less.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><em><span>Note: I’ll be doing a Substack Live at noon with Heather Cox Richardson</span></em></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. The Biden administration alienated a lot of voters by governing far to the left on domestic issues and, while Kamala Harris did turn things around from her dire starting position, it was unwise of Democrats to pick a candidate so closely associated with Joe Biden and doubly unwise of that candidate to do so little to distance herself from Biden on any domestic issues. A repeated pattern in American politics is that when a party loses by being too extreme, their initial reaction is to become even more extreme. Democrats </span><em><span>ought</span></em><span> to move to the center in 2028, but they probably won’t and that’s bad.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But that’s not Marshall’s argument.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead, he’s arguing that the center is getting what it deserves for being insufficiently committed to the fight against Donald Trump and MAGA. And I think that this is wrong. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Rather, it’s the hard left that is taking advantage of the Democratic Party’s current weakened state to advance all-out factional warfare as their top priority, above fighting Trump. Which is just to say, by all means, you should endorse the expenditure of time and attention and resources needed to fight safe-seat primary battles against incumbents who are way too left-wing to win races in Iowa and Texas and Ohio </span><em><span>if you actually agree with the candidates challenging them</span></em><span>. But if your focus is on beating Trump, then admit to yourself that you hold an uncool and somewhat unfashionable set of political priorities and simply disagree with the hottest youth movement in America. Don’t run cover for people who have a different worldview from yours and hope for the best.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Do you want to fight or do you want to win?</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the TV show “Andor” — the best recent art about politics — Diego Luna as the lead character observes, “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/88c5bee0-4d18-4aba-ac3e-8663ec76712f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>We’re in a war. You wanna fight, or do you wanna win?</span></a><span>”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And I think that this is a question I am constantly asking my “Politix” Co-Host Brian Beutler to look into his heart and ponder. Because for the last few years, it really seems to me that for many Democrats, the answer is that they want to fight. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Or, rather, that politics is primarily expressive behavior and their priority in politics is </span><em><span>expressing</span></em><span> their strong dislike of Donald Trump. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s understandable. The United States of America is a nation of individualists. We are also a wealthy society in which most people are living very far from subsistence levels. Most American college graduates, in particular, enjoy a level of material comfort that is inconceivable to most people around the world or throughout human history. Most of us choose jobs and careers that give us not just money but also a sense of self-actualization and value. Politics is becoming more post-material in almost every affluent country. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The United States is unusual, though, in maintaining a strong two-party system. You’re seeing fragmentation in lots of foreign countries, where voters increasingly prioritize the idea of voting for a political party that they feel really speaks for them rather than one that tries to speak for the median voter even if the ultimate outcome is just going to be a coalition deal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I don’t want to claim to be above expressive politics. I really love Green Day, and I think there’s something exhilarating about being in a crowd of people chanting, “no Trump, no K.K.K., no fascist U.S.A.”</span></p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/c8387397-f412-49f4-8ed6-32303f3d716b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/varExpTrTb8" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Wouldn’t it feel awesome if I could watch a politician who I feel as good about as I feel about Green Day? A speech that gave me the vibes of a great concert. That </span><em><span>would</span></em><span> be awesome. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But I have to temper myself and remember that Mary Peltola, James Talarico, Josh Turek, Sherrod Brown, and Roy Cooper have a weighty responsibility on their shoulders. rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“You voted for Trump because of legitimate concerns about Biden’s failures on immigration and inflation, and I hear and acknowledge those concerns, but Trump has betrayed his affordability promises and I can help” is a plausible message for winning over disillusioned Trump voters. “You and the majority of your friends and family voted for a racist, K.K.K.-like fascist movement and now you need to repent” is really not. What’s more, Green Day borrowed the slogan from a more obscure punk band called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/206865ac-bd27-4e38-ae49-42cc6b4ee4cd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>MDC</span></a><span>, an acronym whose meaning has changed over the years but has often stood for Millions of Dead Cops, which is not a great electoral message.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s fun for Graham Platner to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ca843301-0c2f-4e81-a207-8c358d9f3a5f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>campaign with the Dropkick Murphys</span></a><span>, but that’s just another way of saying that expressive politics in blue states is more fun than winning over swing voters. Meanwhile, it turns out that the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/526b5c58-3ab7-414e-afd2-c76c83e7ed09?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>unfun people wringing their hands</span></a><span> about his bad judgement were on to something important. I get why the deeply idiosyncratic people who believe that the benefits of living in New York City exceed the financial costs find it more joyful to participate in Zohran Mamdani’s campaign against Andrew Cuomo than to care about Cait Conley beating an incumbent Republican in the suburbs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it drives me crazy when I see professional political operatives, staffers, and media personalities who happen to be college-educated urbanites treating things like “excitement” and “attention” as if they are wholly exogenous rather than things influential people construct. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If you work in these fields and are </span><em><span>choosing</span></em><span> to be more excited about and pay more attention to politicians who appeal to your social peers than to politicians who appeal to the older, less-credentialed, and dramatically less-urbanized population of swing voters, then that is a decision </span><em><span>you</span></em><span> are making about what’s important in American life today. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think that defeating the MAGA movement is important. I also think that providing health insurance to low-income people by winning power in red states and expanding Medicaid is important. So even though Cooper and Andy Beshear and John Bel Edwards in some sense do not speak directly to my personal tastes, I choose in my capacity as a professional political pundit to treat their work as important and interesting and exciting. Because it </span><em><span>is</span></em><span> important, and because if you can’t find it within yourself to be excited by and interested in the people doing important work, then I don’t understand why you’re in these fields at all.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);"><span>Know when to walk away and know when to run</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Progressive candidates waging factional battles in safe-seat primaries have defined themselves as the true heroes of the Resistance by the sleight of hand of engaging in maximalist anti-Trump position-taking. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, Trump has done bad, cruel things on immigration policy. Democrats should (and largely do) oppose that. But leftists argue that the way to </span><em><span>maximally</span></em><span> oppose Trump on immigration is to refuse to own up to any problems with Biden-era admissions, say that we should “abolish ICE,” or perhaps agree with Avila Chevalier that “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8d959912-9384-4629-8caa-4468c6b63480?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>all deportations are wrong</span></a><span>.” </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Brad Lander recently won a primary against an incumbent House Democrat in Manhattan. By my lights, whatever the substantive differences between Lander and Dan Goldman, the whole idea of spending time and money and resources on something like that is very different from spending time and money and resources on fighting Trump. But Lander’s argument was that the primary was in fact part of a larger battle between “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bfa21da5-89fb-4abe-887e-2c1b5989d639?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>fighters and folders</span></a><span>.” That’s a clever way of getting normal resistance-oriented Democrats to ignore the fact that Lander’s whole campaign was a diversion of resources away from anti-Trump politics and into ideological rigorism. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Because, by definition, if you are dogmatically left-wing, you will be opposed to anything Trump proposes even if it’s extremely popular or makes sense on the merits.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I used to play regularly in a friendly poker game, and I was never very good at it. The reason is that I’d get bored and play way too many hands. I was </span><em><span>aware</span></em><span> that this was bad strategy and would sporadically resolve to do better, but after a beer or two I’d be feeling loose and happy. My discipline would collapse and I’d be playing expressive poker rather than smart poker.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Which is just to say that if you’re trying to win then, as the song says, “You got to know when to hold ’em and know when to fold ’em.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From my perspective as someone who wants to win, the big problem with establishment Democrats is that they’re not folding enough hands. When you insist on fighting Trump on questions like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ba3e93ab-d212-40ab-a231-216c59a86a84?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>who should play on women’s sports teams</span></a><span> or whether you </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0f9754e7-a867-446e-ab65-6c617305e53e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>should need an ID to vote</span></a><span>, you are not playing to win. It’s the establishment that owns that mistake, not the left, but the left </span><em><span>does</span></em><span> keep them pinned down by demanding even more losing fights on questions like ICE. From the left’s viewpoint, this is at least rational because they are sincerely not focused on beating Republicans — that’s why they’re pouring so much energy into beating Democratic incumbents in primaries. And they are enabled in this internecine extravagance and waste by resistance-minded people like Marshall who prioritize “fighting” over playing to win.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" 26px;font-size: 16px;">Today I’m going to do something a little different. I’m going to tell you what I think the debate over GDP is really about.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Free trade usually raises GDP. Immigration, done right, raises GDP.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> Rightists in America want less free trade and less immigration. But every time they propose restricting trade and immigration, someone — either libertarian business/econ types on their own side, or moderate liberals on the other side — says “That will make America poorer!”. So they want some way to neutralize this objection, so they can do things that will, in fact, make America poorer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So America’s right borrowed an argument from the European left. The European left </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dc646ee1-3c84-45f1-b112-c192f3e136b4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">favors degrowth</a><span>, and another term for degrowth is “making GDP go down on purpose”. So naturally, they’re always trying to find reasons to denigrate GDP as a metric of human flourishing (see </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/370ac5f9-ed6c-4434-9725-ab9901014d6f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">here</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7056c82b-0597-4de8-bd16-dc15336046e7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">here</a><span>, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b179091-2573-43e8-adaa-ea316131348a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">here</a><span> for examples). The American right is simply tweaking these arguments to make them more appealing to their own base. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>JD Vance, who has emerged as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ce674a3f-c641-4901-a070-07221bc9e73d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the consensus leader of the New Right</a><span>, makes </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/84c68cd3-6e35-4f53-9e1b-7fc77d10b443?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a bunch of these anti-GDP arguments</a><span> in his new book. For example, he uses the example of Japan to point out that unobserved quality differences in non-traded products can make it difficult to compare GDP across countries:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re focused on GDP, a $6 pint of Japanese strawberries is no different from a $6 pint of American strawberries. If you’re focused on dollars and cents, each contributes equally to the economic indicators. But if everyone in Japan eats better strawberries than everyone in America, the economic indicators have failed to measure something meaningful.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is actually a good argument, and I’ve made it myself many times in the past. I’m in Japan right now, and there actually are a lot of little things that make Japanese products and services a bit nicer than their American counterparts — clean tables at Starbucks, slightly better-tasting food, and so on. Economists who try to adjust for quality differences end up catching some of these things, but probably miss most of them. That ends up </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dcc5988e-9630-4184-a5ea-0fc117e84fa8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">creating a problem</a><span> for GDP comparisons between countries. And it’s only one of many such problems. Comparing lifestyles in countries where life is very different is just </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/83a6a2a8-71e8-418c-8ca1-bf690aeb1b35?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a difficult thing to do</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But instead of simply noting that economics is hard, JD Vance uses this good argument as a reason to bash the entire field of economics:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When I got back home, a friend asked me if I learned anything on my trip to Japan. “Yes,” I replied snidely. “Maybe economics is just fake.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When you read some of Vance’s other arguments against GDP, his agenda becomes clearer:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">[A]s the decline of Christianity has left us without a shared moral language, economics has stepped into the vacuum. We pretend there are scientific answers to questions of values. Take one of the major issues of the 2024 campaign and a significant focus of our time in the White House: Should our trade policy be oriented around protecting domestic industries and jobs or around ensuring a short-term supply of cheap consumer goods?</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This idea — that economists urge values of base consumerism on society, and ignore other moral considerations — is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7d9af42a-9ffd-4495-8348-56a1b5964ad0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">common in European leftist discourse</a><span>. But instead of urging us to care more about inequality, power, and so on, as European leftists do, Vance wants us to care more about spiritual elevation, morality, community — i.e., things that the American right cares about. He goes on to write:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">[W]e now live in a society almost blinded to considerations outside of the economic. This way of thinking is inherently opposed to the Christian way, which demands more focus on people…Take, for instance, the time we spend with our children…Domestic labor—that done by moms and dads—if unpaid, is uncounted in measures like GDP. When I leave work to spend time with my children, when I cook them dinner or argue with them about eating their carrots, I am engaged in economically unproductive work. No money changes hands, so it doesn’t show up in our national figures. By contrast, if I left for dinner at 6 p.m. and returned to work until midnight while paying a total stranger to look after my kid, my contribution to GDP would be much higher.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">and:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you step away from the glory of economic statistics, so much of American life has gone wrong. An influx of prescription opioids became a flood of synthetic opioids, which has led to tens of thousands of deaths each year and a declining life expectancy among a substantial portion of our society. We have made great progress on reducing infant mortality, but we send our children into a world—even in the physical security of their own homes—that bombards them with images and influences that have left them isolated, depressed, and increasingly at risk of self-harm. We are more disconnected, lonely, and isolated, even in the midst of historic levels of material comfort.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">All this economic abundance coexists with intense spiritual misery. We orient people toward a life of consumption. We tell them to find meaning in the home they buy, the money they earn, the prestige of their job. We bombard them with all manner of creature comforts, and add their consumption—price club mega-size junk—to our national GDP. We use that GDP as a yardstick for our broader society, which is why it’s possible for false prophet economists to argue the American Dream is healthy even as suicide and addiction rates soar and the laughter of children fades from our streets.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some of these arguments are — in my opinion — reasonable. A culture of overwork can boost GDP, at least in the short term, at the expense of quality time with family. This is actually a common argument of the center-left, which is why liberals have long fought — often successfully — for </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/356c5d6e-c69d-41dd-941e-6bd753f9ed2a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">more paid family leave</a><span> and other policies that reduce GDP slightly in exchange for more quality time with family. Whether this has increased birth rates isn’t clear — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/14d943db-2654-45c8-b789-8f11237869db?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the evidence is very mixed</a><span> — but it’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cb254f97-ecc8-496a-bc75-6f3b8e1375cf?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a very popular policy</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other arguments are clearly mistaken. Over-prescription of opioids has clearly </span><em>reduced</em><span> GDP, by a massive amount. Yes, selling a bunch of opioid painkillers to Americans </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/139e81a6-5117-4d7d-89a5-80bbeb6163e7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">raises GDP by a few billion dollars</a><span>, but this is vastly outweighed by the trillions of dollars of GDP that we lose from having a bunch more people addicted to painkillers, heroin, and fentanyl. Here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3aa0c662-d6f4-4d12-8f40-025225f7d4fa?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the Philadelphia Fed in 2023</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is growing evidence that the opioid epidemic has harmed many aspects of the real economy, including the labor market, consumer finance, and municipal finance. According to analyses from the Council of Economic Advisers’ 2019 report, the annual (nominal) </span><strong>economic cost of the opioid epidemic</strong><span>, including the cost of lives lost, is estimated at about $700 billion (roughly 3.4 percent of GDP) in 2018 alone, and </span><strong>over $2.5 trillion from 2015 to 2018</strong><span>. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So if you care about GDP, you should view curbing opioid and opiate abuse as a huge priority! Vance is simply not thinking about this very clearly. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Vance’s real problem is that he conflates correlation with causation. In words that could have come straight from the mouth of a European degrowther, he rails against “creature comforts”, “consumption”, and “price club mega-size junk”. But nowhere does he explain why </span><em>depriving</em><span> Americans of these creature comforts would give them closer-knit families, a stronger sense of morality, stronger communities, reduced loneliness, and so on. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why would taking away Americans’ large houses, SUVs, big-screen TVs, or central air conditioning make them spiritually richer? Modern Europe — which JD Vance </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e46f74e3-98e6-4cce-99ed-e9eaaf8f2ab7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">spends much of his time railing against</a><span> — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/83a6a2a8-71e8-418c-8ca1-bf690aeb1b35?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">lacks most of these things</a><span>. And yet America has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/70005918-de11-496a-b1b5-32db8c2fbd65?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">higher fertility rates than Europe</a><span>, we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9c121b87-91e6-420c-bd65-d86b2423c596?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">go to church much more</a><span>, and we have a much more robust social conservative movement. Europe has also been far more restrictive of speech that criticizes Islam, as Vance repeatedly notes. Yes, America has been trending </span><em>away</em><span> from social conservatism and Christianity in recent decades, but so has Europe, and the gap remains. Other developed countries in East Asia — most of which are moderately poorer than the U.S. in GDP terms — are extremely secular. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What about America’s past? We were much poorer in the 1950s, yet we went to church a lot more, had larger families, and so on. If you took away the material gains we’ve made since then, would we go back to tradwives and bowling leagues and lawn parties and Sunday church and 4 kids per family? </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Perhaps, but it’s doubtful. Remember that the 1950s and 1960s were the culmination of a long </span><em>upswing</em><span> of community, religiosity, and so on in American society — something the sociologist Robert Putnam </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/08cbf009-4a98-4d53-9237-3c95c591ee63?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">has documented extensively</a><span>. This is from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a7941e6-3a21-4022-8330-c3c317598559?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a relevant </a><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a7941e6-3a21-4022-8330-c3c317598559?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Works in Progress</a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3a7941e6-3a21-4022-8330-c3c317598559?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"> article</a><span> by Anvar Sarygulov & Phoebe Arslanagic-Little:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Parenthood rapidly became much easier and safer between the 1930s and 1950s. The spread of labour-saving devices in the home such as washing machines and fridges made raising children easier; improvements in medicine making childbirth safer; and easier access to housing made it cheaper to house larger families…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[H]ousehold electrification paved the way for other technologies, including home refrigeration…By the 1940s, electric washing machines were becoming normal in middle class homes…</span><span>Between 1936 and 1956, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ad7a3feb-719e-4070-b4e6-2f3da1f7d35a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">America’s</a><span> maternal death rate fell by 94 percent, from 51 deaths per 10,000 live births to under 3…[M]edical advances, which were being made across the West, radically reduced the most serious potential cost faced by prospective mothers: life itself…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Alongside strides forward in household and medical technology…[I]t became easier to secure a home in which to raise children. The number of houses built soared across the West after World War Two…This house-building bonanza led to sharp rises in homeownership rates.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The golden thread linking the phenomena that comprise the triple mechanism we describe above – advances in household technology, progress in medical technology, and easier access to housing – is that they together </span><strong><span>sharply reduced the cost of having children</span></strong><span>. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you like the kind of society we had in 1960, you can’t ignore the story of how we got to 1960. The answer was “economic growth”. This, combined with the examples of Europe and Asia, is why there’s no reason to believe that forcing Americans to be poorer — taking away the “creature comforts” Vance despises — would lead us to suddenly rediscover the value of community, family, and religion. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now it’s worth noting that if you were to decrease America’s GDP to poor-country levels — below $15,000 per person, as opposed to over $90,000 today — you might be able to raise fertility. women can’t read or write, and infant mortality is so high that families have to have many kids as a form of insurance — tend to have above-replacement fertility (though some don’t). But even this law is weakening, as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/afa9d7a7-9947-4b66-9ebd-ea9cc82e82d5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">fertility rates in Sub-Saharan Africa plunge</a><span>, so even that extreme level of GDP reduction would probably fail to restore high fertility over the long run. Also, I kind of doubt that JD Vance wants to force Americans to live lives similar to those lived in Sub-Saharan Africa.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What about JD Vance’s preferred policies — trade protectionism and immigration reduction? Would those restore American community, family, and religion, at the expense of a bit of GDP? As I said earlier, that’s actually what I think this whole debate is really about. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On trade, you’ve seen Trump explicitly make the argument that Americans are going to need to suffer a bit of material deprivation in order to achieve the administration’s goals:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/7c677185-79b2-4e08-af5c-5ae13a2fe081?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/2eJv810QWOs" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But how will doing this restore community, family, etc.? Presumably you could make an argument that protectionism will bring back good manufacturing jobs, which will then give men the confidence and social standing they need to get married and have kids. There’s just one big problem with this, though: </span><strong>Trump’s trade policy doesn’t actually increase the number of good manufacturing jobs</strong><span>. We’ve lost manufacturing jobs since Trump took office last year!</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure href="https://substack.com/redirect/ca09dea0-342e-41bc-9a2f-d132f20e5936?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Trump’s tariffs are hurting the U.S. manufacturing sector</a><span>, by raising the cost of intermediate goods. Economists understand this pretty well; JD Vance, who thinks “economics is just fake”, does not seem to understand it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>How about immigration? Rightists will endlessly cite Robert Putnam’s finding that diversity reduces social trust in American communities. But as Bryan Caplan and many others </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3497096f-a674-4361-8d42-e42ab0dbae02?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">have pointed out</a><span>, the effect size is tiny — in Putnam’s research, going from </span><em>zero</em><span> diversity to </span><em>maximum</em><span> diversity reduces social trust by the equivalent of 1 point on a 100-point scale. This suggests that all the mass deportations in the world won’t move the needle on American community and togetherness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, JD Vance’s crusade against GDP is a </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d99a74ee-670d-48e8-be51-740836409af6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">cargo cult</a></em><span>. Sure, GDP doesn’t measure “the beauty of our poetry or the strength of our marriages,” to use Robert F. Kennedy’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/69177737-0744-45c4-9c5d-d2a3fe62e4bb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">famous words</a><span>. But that doesn’t mean that making Americans poorer will make their poetry more beautiful or their marriages stronger. Nor does it mean that policies that also happen to make us a bit poorer, like immigration reduction or tariffs, are any more likely to strengthen our society. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a famous episode of </span><em>Star Trek: The Next Generation</em><span> — my favorite TV show of all time — Captain Picard castigates an alien for turning his society into a fascist empire. When the alien responds that the fascist government’s forced modernization program raised his daughter out of poverty, Picard responds with the beautiful quote at the top of this post: “Her belly may be full, but her spirit will be empty.” But was Picard arguing that it was</span><em> the full bellies themselves</em><span> that emptied the people’s spirits? Was he merely arguing that the fascist empire ought to become a </span><em>poorer</em><span> fascist empire, in order to restore the virtue of the people? Only a fool would think so. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Look, I also want America to have a stronger society. I want us to have more kids. I want us to have more stable families. I want us to have closer-knit communities, better moral values, etc. But that doesn’t mean the New Right knows how to get us there. So far, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b0dc466-d194-45ae-9ffe-7132c9210b48?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the New Right has built nothing</a><span> — no new community organizations or institutions, no religious revival, nothing that would knit our society together. It has merely thrashed and thrashed against modernity, with no plan for a replacement. JD Vance’s crusade against GDP is simply more of the same.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: 10px;">“Done right” means getting immigrants who, on average, earn more than the native-born. This raises GDP by a composition effect — you have richer people on average. It also probably raises GDP by other means — increasing market size which increases returns to scale, boosting innovation and entrepreneurship, and so on. If you get mostly low-skilled immigrants, things get dicier — the composition effect reduces GDP because you’re importing poorer people, but the increased market size may still cancel that out. But in general, if you want higher per capita GDP, you should be selective in terms of who you let into the country. Total GDP, of course, is a different matter — if you want a bigger country, in order to be more powerful in military terms, then letting in tons of low-skilled immigrants may be worth it even if they reduce per capita GDP. And of course, there are distributional reasons to allow in low-skilled immigration — eldercare and so on. But basically, if you let in high-skilled immigrants, your society gets richer by pretty much every metric.</p></div></div></div></div><table class="email-ufi-2-bottom" role="presentation" But even that one is about a cannibalistic serial killer. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In more recent times, though, Baltimore is best known (at least among policy heads) for one of the most remarkable crime drops in America. the public officials who spearheaded this would be famous national heroes, but Mayor Brandon Scott hasn’t really gotten the credit he deserves. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That reflects, to an extent, some of his communications decisions. He talks about “gun violence” rather than crime, and his signature anti-crime initiative is called the Group Violence Reduction Strategy, avoiding the word “gang.” </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the actual upshot of Scott-era policy has not been to replace group violence inflicted by firearms with classy, Hannibal Lecter-style solo non-gun killings. There’s just less crime. And while I wish Scott would communicate about this somewhat differently, the thing that really matters here is the results, which are very good, and I want more people to understand how they came about because I think they’re broadly replicable in other large cities. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Baltimore is also interesting for some of its not-so-replicable qualities, though. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are lots of American cities where ideally we’d see less crime. But Charm City is a place that is </span><em>uniquely</em><span> hobbled by crime, not just in the sense that crime is high but in the sense that the basic fundamentals on housing, jobs, and the built environment are otherwise pretty strong. A sustained low-crime spell in Baltimore could easily set off a positive cycle of in-migration and investment that unlocks a ton of new appealing neighborhoods and generates huge gains. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The Baltimore context</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On the politics, Scott is an interesting case because he was elected in 2020 after a series of corruption scandals rocked the city’s political establishment. Against the backdrop of the Great Awokening, he positioned himself as a young progressive rather than a tough-on-crime candidate, which is probably one reason he hasn’t gotten the national press attention he deserves. Another notable thing is that if you look at the chart, Baltimore just skipped the entire murder surge that afflicted most of America in 2020 and 2021.</p><div class="paywall-jump" href="https://substack.com/redirect/3e5abdad-414e-4d86-9ff5-25c3d1c35c78?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">ended with no style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This was an all-around odd time in the politics of American crime. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In Ferguson, Mo., we also saw the </span><a
