Department conclude that no charges were warranted</a><span> against the officer who shot Michael Brown, along with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f504f5c3-139c-4b5a-af6a-c1907a02fab1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">substantial rioting</a><span> and a localized increase in crime. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As the late </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3b38ea71-3c4c-498a-a892-bc78f7759037?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Richard Rosenfeld rightly complained</a><span>, official crime data is reported with far too long a lag for people to actually know with any confidence in 2016 or 2017 whether it was true that St. Louis and Baltimore were experiencing localized homicide surges due to reductions in the intensity of police effort. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I believe this is clearly true in retrospect (per </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c5b69da7-e0ba-45e1-b6a9-0486b99c95c6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">the Devi and Fryer research</a><span>), and American progressives should have known this by 2020 but were kind of in denial. At the time of the 2016 election, it was a bit of a hot take that lacked clear empirical support.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Back to Baltimore, though. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The city’s huge crime surge in 2015 undid 20 years’ worth of slow, steady progress against murder, and crime then plateaued at a high level. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One consequence was that Baltimore didn’t have major anti-police protests in 2020 or big new explicit (or implicit) policy changes. Scott was kind of a Great Awokening progressive, but he was also running in a city that was already four and a half years into a vicious crime surge, so being anti-crime was part of his politics from the beginning. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meanwhile, in 2022 Baltimore </span><em>did</em><span> have a tough-on-crime backlash as Marilyn Mosby — the progressive prosecutor who charged but then failed to convict the Freddie Gray cops and who also had some unrelated scandals — was defeated by Ivan Bates, who offered a back-to-basics anti-crime message. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Bates and Scott seem to have a bad relationship in which their fighting each other for political credit is making it harder for either of them to get the credit that they want and deserve. They might want to take P.R. lessons from San Francisco, where it’s true that both Dan Lurie and Brooke Jenkins sort of lowkey jostle for credit but are also basically saying the same thing and are visibly cooperating in a way that makes it easier to tell a San Francisco success story. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">My verdict on the evidence, though, is pretty clear: Bates is right that replacing Mosby with a competent prosecutor who has a normal working relationship with the police department was a necessary and important reset. He’s also right that Scott has not discovered some kind of magical alternative to the traditional work of police and prosecutors. At the same time, the Baltimore crime decline is much steeper than a “return to normal” and is much larger in extent than the national trend. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">You can’t explain an extraordinary effect by citing a normal cause. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Normalcy (i.e., Bates) accounts for quantitatively the largest slice of the crime decline but what’s unusual (i.e., Scott) accounts for the part of the decline that’s most interesting. So I don’t mean to slight Bates, who I think is basically correct — I’ve written a bunch of articles (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e50e0005-d4ec-45b1-83c0-5b1851fd3366?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">one</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/09feb9e9-bc65-44f4-b1c7-267a7856f450?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">two</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/50a83901-2f0e-40cd-b0ee-a053e5fe433a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">three</a><span>) about the importance of conventional proactive policing. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the rest of </span><em>this</em><span> article is about focused deterrence. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Focused deterrence in Baltimore </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The strategy of focused deterrence comes out of work that was pioneered in Boston in the 1990s by criminologist David Kennedy; I learned about this from Paul Grogan’s 2001 book “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/737f602e-bece-4fa6-8f3e-337bc79fcb3d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Comeback Cities</a><span>.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The basic idea is that a large fraction of urban shootings are quasi-predictable. Not pre-crime exactly, but predictable in the sense that gangs participate in regular spirals of retaliatory violence. Somebody will get shot or at least shot at. That somebody is a person who himself has a long record of arrests and associates who’ve also been arrested multiple times in the past. Whether or not you can prove beyond a reasonable doubt who exactly shot him — and especially whether or not you can prove that the shooter had accomplices — it is knowable via intelligence gathering which crew it is that people believe the shooter belonged to and who, broadly speaking, is in that crew. You do not need psychic powers to understand that the most likely series of events going forward involves members of the victim’s crew taking shots at members of the perpetrator’s crew, and then members of that crew shooting back. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/582ae1fe-6094-4a18-bb88-f50ea3ab1c3d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Jeremy Biddle and Ben Struhl in Vital City</a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ac54cb03-c5fd-4aee-a66e-62d02d2df62c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Charles Lehman in the Free Press</a><span> offer slightly different accounts of how this works, reflecting the fact that the former are academics and the latter is a conservative think tanker. But they’re really saying the same thing. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the focused deterrence model, you attempt to (a) gather timely intelligence about these predictable cycles of violence and (b) move decisively to prevent them. Step (b) involves delivering somewhat individualized messages to the people who the authorities believe are likely to be victims or perpetrators of crime:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">We know you are mixed up in the life.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">We know your life may be at risk. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>We want </span><em>you</em><span> to know that we’re watching you, and if you do crime you will be caught and punished.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">We also want you to know that there’s an alternative to being a perpetrator or a victim: getting out of the life.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">We are prepared to help you with (4), if you want. </p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In terms of the debates over whether you reduce crime with services or enforcement, I think what’s important about the focused deterrence model is that from the point of view of the state, you’re doing both. The goal is to present “services or enforcement” as a choice </span><em>to the potential shooter</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I have personally been on a journey with focused deterrence. I read Grogan’s book in college and was totally pilled on it. The late Mark Kleiman, who was a major early influence on my crime thinking, was also a proponent. But then </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a038304e-13ea-4375-9c28-20b108e6af1a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Jennifer Doleac</a><span> convinced me the evidence base for Operation Ceasefire in Boston was actually low-quality. There were also examples of other cities, including Baltimore, saying they were going to do focused deterrence and then not seeing strong results. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Something that Scott deserves a lot of credit for is that he not only spearheaded a program that has worked well, but he also worked with smart academics to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bb83161c-3274-4f50-a500-354644062644?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">build a rigorous research design into it</a><span>, so there’s now much better evidence that it is working. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The other thing Scott deserves credit for (but that also serves as a cautionary note) is that doing focused deterrence at large scale is hard. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s easy to </span><em>say</em><span> you’re going to do this. But a lot of cities have made failed efforts where the quality of the intelligence isn’t very good, where the call-ins involve excessively large groups of people, and where as a result the deterrence methods aren’t credible. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This can easily collapse, in practice, to a kind of “call in the usual suspects” and have social service providers wander around uselessly. But while police don’t need conviction-quality evidence to say to a group of young men, “Hey, we basically know what’s going on here and we’ve got our eyes on you so don’t fuck around but </span><em>do</em><span> reach out and accept our help,” they do need to actually know what’s going on. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Part of the Baltimore success is that they’re able to do this because they started in just one part of the city; even now, it hasn’t scaled up to every police district. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Fundamentally, though, the point is that a very large share of homicides consists of criminals shooting at other criminals. Because the victims are not necessarily super-sympathetic and their friends aren’t interested in cooperating with police, these things can just proceed on a low boil for a long time. But plenty of innocent bystanders end up getting hurt, a much larger range of innocent bystanders is terrified, and each expansion of killing risks drawing more young men into violent gangs for protection and solidarity. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Baltimore’s bright future</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The upshot of all of this is that I am quite bullish on the city of Baltimore. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lots of high-crime cities are also enmeshed in much larger regional problems that are not necessarily amenable to solution by city government. Places like Detroit, St. Louis, and Cleveland are dealing with issues that are downstream of global economic forces. But Maryland is always contending with New Jersey and Massachusetts for the status of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2bfd5b00-3303-415b-9b60-44ab089612c9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">number one in median household income</a><span>. The Baltimore metro area has a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/890cf3df-74c2-4cf0-85a0-6f8d68146cce?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">higher median household income</a><span> than Dallas, Austin, or Atlanta. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The issue is that Baltimore City specifically is poor compared to nearby counties:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px should of course adopt YIMBY reforms. But in the Maryland context, “why don’t you move to the cheap city instead” isn’t like suggesting that people live in Syracuse rather than Brooklyn. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Baltimore is not isolated from job opportunities. It’s literally in the center of an affluent metro area in a rich state! </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/22192d54-78e2-4cb7-a116-febeb7c9beb4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Every workday,</a><span> about 85,000 Baltimoreans commute out of the city to jobs in the suburbs and about 200,000 people commute into the city from the suburbs. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Marginal population growth in Baltimore could occur entirely from people who already have jobs in the city and just want a cheaper place to live. They are currently deterred by high crime and bad schools. Schools are a tough problem, but there are tens of thousands of childless young people in the Baltimore metro area and also tens of thousands of vacant homes and vacant lots in Baltimore City. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you can get 100 current commuters to live in the city instead, that creates additional jobs in the city providing locally facing services and that increases demand for city living. Ultimately, you have to address the schools and make the city more family-friendly. But from a fiscal standpoint, childless employed people are actually ideal because they consume fewer city services. Population growth would make it easy to reduce Baltimore’s property taxes, which would encourage rehabbing more of the city’s vacant lots and structures. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a virtuous circle in which lower crime means more residents means more local jobs means lower taxes means more residents. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The 1990s crime decline saw </span><em>some</em><span> of that virtuous circle happening, but at that point Baltimore was actually something of a laggard relative to the general trend toward lower crime in American cities. This time, they are leaders. And because Baltimore has also been less impacted by the prior gentrification of other East Coast cities, there’s more low-hanging housing fruit to pick. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There will probably be some recognition lag before people find out the good news about Baltimore, but if public officials stay the course, I think the city has a bright future.</p><p class="button-wrapper" underline;">subscribe on YouTube</a><span>.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Transcript</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Donald Trump has distinguished himself in many ways. One of them is that he is our first pump and dump president. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hi, Paul Krugman here. A podcast today rather than a full-on piece: I’m a little exhausted from number-crunching over the weekend. So I thought I’d talk briefly about the really extraordinary financial picture that we’re seeing under the current administration.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Obviously no president has enriched himself from office the way that Trump has. That’s common knowledge. One of the things that is really amazing about it, however, is the way in which he enriched himself — a lot of which has to do with crypto.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So the New York Times had a report just the other day on Trumpcoin, the memecoin issued on Trump’s behalf which got a lot of buyers, a lot of money came flowing into it. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It should have been obvious from the beginning that the coin was inherently worthless, and at this point it essentially is worthless. It has lost 97 percent of its value. But a lot of people did buy in at the high prices.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What was special about the New York Times story was two things. First, they put a number on how much money naive investors have lost on the coin, which is 3.8 billion dollars. And even more surprising is the number of people who were in effect suckers here — almost a million.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s really amazing. I mean, I was completely cynical but I didn’t think there were that many suckers out there. But it turns out there were really a lot. A few people made money off the coin — basically insiders who got to buy it early and then were able to cash in before the broader retail market realized that this was a worthless token. There’s another token, the World Liberty Financial coin — which has also crashed, although the Times had difficulty in tracking down how many people have lost how much money. There’s the Melania coin. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Okay, all of this is amazing. As Trump would say, it’s like nothing anybody’s ever seen before. I think we should say, however, that this is a bigger story than just the Trump coin, and it’s a bigger story than just Trump himself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What we’re witnessing is or has been a really enormous pump and dump scheme, I would argue, involving more or less all of crypto. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So if you don’t know the background, Trump used to be highly critical of cryptocurrency, saying it was worthless and a scam, which was true. But then when it became clear that there was money in it for him, he reversed course. And during the 2024 election, crypto interests contributed a lot of money to Trump. They then after the election poured a lot of money into his own enrichment, into his own projects. And the administration came in with a very pro crypto stance: deregulation encouraging uses of crypto, at least talk about a national bitcoin reserve, all of that. And the price of bitcoin doubled after the election; the valuation, the market cap of cryptocurrency in general went from a little over two trillion to more than four trillion.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And then starting last fall it all came crashing down. Not all the way to zero — the price of Bitcoin right now as I record this is about what it was on the eve of the 2024 election; it’s about half what it was at its peak. That’s also true, roughly speaking for the market cap. So we’ve seen about two trillion dollars of market valuation wiped out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why is this a pump and dump story? Well what is cryptocurrency good for? As you know, I’ve been on this for a long time. Bitcoin was introduced in 2009 — this is a seventeen year old idea which has yet to find any legitimate use cases. Illegitimate use cases, yes. There was also a report in the Wall Street Journal about the extent to which Iran and North Korea have been making use of cryptocurrency to evade U.S. sanctions, so there is that. But it’s still not enough to justify a multi-trillion dollar asset.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anyway, it was trendy, it was exciting, it was fashionable and particularly after November 2024 it was pushed with the encouragement of the Trump Administration. It was just a heavy marketing campaign that had the advantage of also having the authority or whatever, the credibility — such as it was but among some people real —of Donald Trump behind it. They all evaporated.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think we can say that to some extent what happened was that Trump kind of moved on to other things. There also is some distracted boyfriend meme: the guy looking over his shoulder. A lot of the excitable, fear of missing out, latest thing money has probably moved from crypto to AI. So that might have happened even without Trump. But the basic story is that Trump guided, pushed people into a whole asset class, crypto, of which a large part is Bitcoin, but other stuff as well. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We don’t know how much, or I don’t know, how much crypto was bought during this period, but it has to be substantial. And then it crashed. And at this point, essentially anybody who bought crypto during this era, since the 2024 election, has lost money.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s a  lot of money; we know that on paper — it’s not really paper, but anyway — in principle two trillion dollars has been lost in crypto. Now a lot of that is probably money just given back, imaginary gains that took place during the run-up. But a substantial amount of additional money was from people who did buy in during this whole episode. So this has to be many times the size of the losses on the Trump coin.  And it is, I would say, at a functional level another pump and dump scheme.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this case the beneficiaries were people who were already in crypto. Clearly some of the crypto interests that bought themselves a president probably stayed fully invested. But others must have cashed out, and a lot of innocents — well a lot of a lot of suckers, let’s not mince words here — a lot of suckers clearly lost a lot of money.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s an extraordinary thing. There have been pump and dump schemes forever, probably going back to the Phoenicians or something. But this is on a scale we’ve never seen, and with the president of the United States in the center of it. Which I guess given everything else comes as no surprise.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Happy 250th birthday, America.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. Brown</a><span>/Contributor via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I did a panel with Adam Gray and Tom Suozzi at WelcomeFest where they outlined their </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/274dfa98-2b00-4216-b3a0-24e18f1e3884?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Promise to America</a><span>, an effort to put some meat on the bones of the general idea of moderation. One of the things they say is “we are capitalist, not socialist,” which is definitely a sentiment that I agree with.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Suozzi said on the panel, very correctly, that market economies have dramatically outperformed the competition and delivered, while not perfect societies, certainly the greatest levels of material prosperity that we see anywhere on Earth. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is all totally correct, but I think that people who know that it’s correct need to think more about why, despite its correctness, it has become so unfashionable for young people to embrace capitalism. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think one really important reason is that if you look at what people spend money on, you know housing and health care are the two most important sectors by far. Young people consume far below-average amounts of health care, though, meaning that their consumption is really dominated by housing. A large share of the population consumes housing in the form of renting a home from themselves, so they are somewhat insulated from the ups and downs of the housing market. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But those people are mostly old. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re young, your experience of the economy is dominated by the housing situation. And the housing situation in the United States is not very good. So I think for most young people “capitalism” means something like “the status quo system,” and they perceive the status quo system to be pretty bad because they are super exposed to the single most dysfunctional element of the status quo economic system. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, in my capacity as a lawyer for capitalism, I am happy to point out that not only is housing the most dysfunctional element of the status quo economy, </span><em>but</em><span> </span><em>it’s also the element that is run in the least capitalistic way</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Far and away the number one thing that could improve young people’s living standards in America would be to embrace more market-oriented housing policies. But for anyone to understand that, those inclined to tout the virtues of capitalism need to embrace that idea. As a political pragmatist, I don’t really blame Suozzi for blasting efforts to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a6218d3-864d-4332-a0d7-67ab02cd67af?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">foist zoning reform on his constituents on Long Island</a><span> a few years ago since his district is a wretched hive of NIMBYism. But younger people’s lived experience of “capitalism” is of central planning and massive shortages of the single most important item they consume. So of course if people tell them the alternative to the status quo is “socialism,” a lot of them are going to want that. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">America’s slow-motion housing crisis </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, on one level, housing in the United States </span><em>is</em><span> very capitalistic. The overwhelming majority of it is constructed with private capital and sold or rented for profit. Most homes are also privately owned — mostly by owner-occupants but with a significant sector of small-time landlords and a handful of large-scale ones, too. Public and nonprofit housing do exist in the United States, but they are a relatively small niche. The result is a housing sector awash in private capital and profit-seeking. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What it lacks is much in the way of free markets. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And these anti-market policies have grown up, over time, in insidious ways and merged to create a situation where, by 2026, we are dealing with systemic housing shortages almost everywhere in the country. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This mess all goes back 100 years to the Supreme Court’s Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty decision, which determined that it is perfectly legitimate to make apartment buildings illegal on certain swaths of land. This is just a huge contravention of the basic logic of free enterprise. It’s not that everyone — or even most people, or even a particularly large minority of people — ought to live in multi-family dwellings. But a small apartment on cheap land is an obvious method of housing low-income people, and low-income people need places to live. And where land is </span><em>expensive</em><span>, stacking dwellings vertically is the most normal and obvious way to ensure that supply and demand curves can balance out. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But widespread midcentury apartment bans did not produce an acute crisis, because of the widespread adoption of the automobile. The fact that it was newly feasible to build much more suburban housing was a huge positive shock to supply in the postwar generation, and that development more than outweighed the impact of bad policy. By the late 1960s, much of this new suburban housing was manufactured homes built in factories. In the 1970s, however, new rules went into effect that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bd4b7433-b1f2-40c2-b251-c71ca70b4fd1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">greatly restricted manufactured housing</a><span>. The late 1970s and the 1980s then saw the rise of the “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/154c0082-c6cc-4062-a732-634413b1454a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">growth control</a><span>” movement in the Northeast and California, which sought to halt suburban sprawl in the name of preserving open space. So by the 1990s, you couldn’t build apartments or manufactured homes on most land, and you couldn’t build suburban sprawl around San Francisco or Los Angeles or New York or Boston. But in </span><em>most</em><span> of America, a metro area could grow outward and housing remained relatively affordable. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Then, after 2008, a consensus developed that too many people were getting mortgages, so we made it harder to finance new suburban starter homes on top of everything else. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For a little while the impact of this wasn’t so notable, but for the past decade or so — since the labor market normalized — we’ve been living in a kind of Everywhere Shortage. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My account of the phases of this crisis follows the work of Kevin Erdmann, who </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a7694a7-07bb-41b1-bd0d-b6c9b3840c8a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">calculates that we’re about 15 million total units short</a><span>. Erdmann was also the first to observe the importance of incorporating events such as the 1970s crackdown on manufactured homes into our understanding of the lead-up to the Great Recession.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the upshot is that we’re in a really bad situation in this country.</p><p class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Ideas versus vibes</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Notably, the people who constructed America’s system of widespread comprehensive central planning of the housing market did not typically think of themselves as socialists. And certainly, the typical suburban homeowner regards it as his God-given right to block new development and change in his neighborhood. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re an older, reasonably prosperous homeowner, this bad situation probably doesn’t have a negative impact on you. And you almost certainly don’t think of yourself as a communist who strongly favors central planning and believes free markets are nonsense. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re a young person facing higher rents and despairing about getting on the path to homeownership, you probably don’t think of yourself as a victim of a failed socialist economic experiment the way a refugee fleeing Cuba or Venezuela would. The victims of bad housing policy hear people talking about how America is a great free-market success story, so if they feel that the success story is not working for them personally, they conclude that capitalism and free markets are in fact a big failure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I would also note that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act passed with overwhelming bipartisan support, but </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/71c0c186-5ab9-445e-94c0-f0f9ed6bd497?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">all of the “no” votes came from Republicans</a><span>. And what those Republicans were objecting to was not the NEPA waivers, manufactured-home deregulation, or regulatory favors for community banks — it was some fairly small incentives to try to get localities to change their zoning. One of the main reasons that statewide zoning reforms keep failing in the Northeast is that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/358b95ea-c12f-42ec-bb07-7fe8f5bc4803?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Acela Corridor Republicans oppose them</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In Maine and New Hampshire and California, Republicans have seen YIMBYism as a form of deregulation and backed it, so big bills have passed. But in New York and Maryland and New Jersey and Connecticut, they’ve seen it as trampling on the sanctity of local control, and it’s been very hard to get anything done. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These are the most invisible people in the discourse relative to their practical significance in American politics. Not just because they directly block housing (though they do block housing), but because politically cautious moderate Democrats fear a backlash </span><em>from the right</em><span> if they embrace housing deregulation. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Obviously, I do not agree with right-NIMBYs on the merits. But they are important, and I think there is remarkably little engagement with their views. What you tend to get is either name-calling leftists asserting these types are racist, or else Manhattan Institute types rationalizing away the bad behavior of northeastern Republicans. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It seems to me, though, that if you want to understand youth socialism, you need to understand why middle-aged and elderly conservatives see opposition to new housing as consistent with their support for capitalism. In their view when you buy a home in a single-family neighborhood, part of what you are buying is the single-familyness of the entire neighborhood. Left-NIMBYs see zoning reform as free-market deregulation, so they are against it. But right-NIMBYs see zoning reform as contravening their property rights, so they are against it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The truth is, this kind of dispute speaks to issues that long predate the whole idea of socialism. It’s an older one about what property rights even are.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The war for simple property rights</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you go back to the emergence of what we understand as capitalism, the prior system was, of course, not socialism but feudalism. And a key aspect of pre-capitalist property rights is that they tended to be very complicated. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In Jane Austen’s Regency-era novels, the characters are constantly grappling with parcels of land that are encumbered by complicated entailments. By our modern lights, the idea that Mr. Bennet could be prohibited from leaving his estate to his daughters is bizarre. It’s either his estate or it’s not. But the traditional mode of thinking was that if an estate is someone’s property, then he has the right to attach whatever kind of stipulation to his property that he wants. When the property is then inherited by someone new, that person inherits the stipulations. To say everyone can do whatever they want with the property that they own would be a major violation of property rights because property rights include the right to impose these irrevocable stipulations. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Thinking about it logically, if entailments can attach to a piece of property but can never be removed, then over the long term all property will be encumbered — and over time it will be encumbered by an increasing number of stipulations. Eventually, all commerce will be strangled by the whims of various long-dead previous owners. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What happened instead was that over the course of the 19th century, various acts of Parliament restricted entailments. And the whole process of creating capitalism was full of measures like this. Pre-modern property rights were very complicated. People had joint shares in communally owned fields. There were all kinds of complicated partial-use rights to various parcels of land that couldn’t be bought or sold. Simplifying these rights made it much easier to undertake various kinds of transactions and engage in modern commerce and growth. Because the British political system of the time was elite-dominated, this was often done on inequitable terms. But it unleashed a ton of growth and made the vast majority of people better off on average. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the modern world, we have recreated a system of complicated property rights. The conventional understanding is that owning a parcel of residential land gives you extensive authority to veto things that your neighbors might want to do, such as redevelop their parcel as townhouses or a small apartment building. In exchange for getting those rights vis-a-vis your neighbors, you lose the right to do what you want with your own land. The people who like the status quo mostly don’t conceive of it as a statist imposition on their personal property rights; they see it as property rights functioning naturally. And the young renters who are locked out of economic opportunity by the status quo </span><em>also</em><span> see this as property rights functioning naturally, and thus they become socialists. But the thing that would solve this problem is not a giant, economically wasteful program of public housing construction. It’s shifting to a regime of simplified property rights where everyone has much less authority over their neighbors’ land and much more authority over their own. </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Capitalism needs boldness and vision</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On the left, there’s a longstanding view that “abundance” and “YIMBYs” are just sock puppets for billionaires trying to bolster the legitimacy of capitalism. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">To this I say — if only! </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s genuinely true that it would do enormous good for the interests of America’s billionaires and C.E.O.s to see radical housing reform sweep the country. That’s in part because faster economic growth is good for everyone, including billionaires and C.E.O.s. But it’s mostly because, exactly as the leftists fear, housing abundance (and its natural complements like abundance of transportation and electricity transmission infrastructure) would bolster the legitimacy of capitalism. If “capitalism” meant “a system where demand for housing is met by rising quantities of housing rather than rising prices of housing,” then a lot more people would enjoy capitalism. But in a world where “capitalism” means “policy defers to the most risk-averse incumbent homeowners around,” a lot of people naturally feel that capitalism is not working for them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But YIMBYism is dramatically worse-funded than the various NIMBY community groups that are propped up by mainstream foundations. Businesses lobby furiously on picayune regulations and tax policy matters, but the collective action problem in lobbying for housing reform is hard to overcome. And politically engaged venture capitalists and C.E.O.s are much more inclined to whine on Twitter about anti-capitalism than to cut large checks to the people trying to make capitalism actually work. I can’t think of any examples of someone pumping money into a primary that features a YIMBY Republican state legislator trying to give the boot to a NIMBY incumbent. For all the discussion of these issues over the past few years, there is still remarkably little money going into the relevant advocacy. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And this creates a dilemma for moderate Democrats. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Part of the point of moderation is to be politically savvy and politically cautious, and obviously calling for large-scale land-use reforms is risky. But another part of the point of moderation is to solve actual problems rather than being trapped by ideological dogmas. It just happens to both be true that capitalism + a welfare state is a much better system than socialism, and also that the economic status quo is not working well for young people. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The good news for markets is that the specific thing that’s not working well is housing — and housing is a problem where the solution is more markets. But this is only going to be persuasive if people are willing to say it and really push to do something about it. There is risk in pushing for big change, but there are also clearly a lot of people who are sick of the status quo and eager to see big change. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Should that change be socialism? Or should it be solving the problem at hand? I know what I think. </p><p class="button-wrapper" Commons</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Back in the 2010s, a lot of people marveled at China’s seemingly recession-proof economy. Throughout the global financial crisis of 2008 and the Chinese stock market crash and capital flight of 2015, the country never recorded a single quarter of negative economic growth. Here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d672ad32-97e9-4a50-8efe-9f8a1be31c67?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">what I wrote back in 2019</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>China’s government seems to have developed a highly effective </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3fdd00d4-ec05-4cd8-9892-e68b402d55c4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">new form</a><span> of economic stabilization. Its extensive control of the financial system allows it to turn on a flood of bank loans when the economy looks weak, and restrain credit when the danger has passed. China’s avoidance of recession in at least the past three decades suggests that this form of credit-based stabilization is more effective than traditional, more indirect stimulation of the economy through government deficits and central bank monetary easing…When a recession threatens, the government tells banks to lend --— to local governments, construction companies and real estate developers. Then, if the credits go bad, the government swoops in and takes the nonperforming loans off of financial companies’ books. Uninterrupted rapid growth then shrinks the government debt as a percentage of gross domestic product, and the system sails blithely forward[.]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And here’s what I wrote in 2018:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>China…directed banks to lend lots more money [in 2009]. The World Bank </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f4e6f344-6add-40a3-a836-698c57dcbca8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">estimated</a><span> that increased bank credit represented 40 percent of China’s stimulus. Much of the lending </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/76e5382e-3e7b-4baf-ad22-c502830c13f7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">was done</a><span> by China’s four large state-owned banks. The money went to infrastructure, real estate and all kinds of corporate projects, many of which were carried out by the country’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ef1251de-b80e-475c-acec-da83b7ee9f13?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">state-owned</a><span> enterprises.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Basically, most countries use two types of policy to get the economy moving again when some sort of negative shock hits it: </p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">monetary policy (e.g. cutting interest rates), and</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">fiscal policy (e.g. stimulus spending).</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Macroeconomists disagree about why interest rate cuts give the economy a boost, but most agree that the policy usually has an effect. Although there are many other theories and interpretations, one way you can think of rate cuts is as a </span><em>financial </em><span>policy — by making it easier for businesses to borrow and invest, low interest rates stimulate business activity. Fiscal policy, in contrast, pretty much bypasses the world of finance and aims directly at the real economy — you build a bridge or a road, which employs some people who might otherwise be unemployed, and then those people turn around and spend their money elsewhere in the economy, igniting a virtuous cycle of spending and working. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>China uses both of those, but it also uses a third policy: </span><em>financial</em><span> policy. Instead of simply cutting interest rates and hoping that this filters through to bank lending, China’s government uses its direct control over the banking system to push banks to lend more. In the 2010s, after the Great Recession and the 2015 Chinese stock crash, this mostly meant lending to real estate companies. This lending fueled the biggest property boom the world has ever seen. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The boom </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4d4a7568-6d0e-4ed7-b977-42ab8621f0a7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">ended in late 2021</a><span>. The crash of the Chinese property developer Evergrande began a sequence of bankruptcies and defaults across the entire real estate sector. China’s property prices began to fall, and have not stopped falling to this day:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px They will point out that productivity is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e4b9bc65-c591-4a44-96be-6c63c75f0afc?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">hard to measure</a><span>; that long-term costs are both uncertain and hard to verify; and that long-term problems can always be fixed later. The more important fact, they’ll argue, is that China did exactly what Xi Jinping said it would do — to pivot away from an excessive reliance on real estate without causing the economy to shrink. “Chinamaxxers” will use this as reason to crow about the superiority of the Chinese way, while left-leaning intellectuals will use China’s performance as a foil to demonstrate the benefits of greater government control over the economy. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s just one problem with this triumphalism: China </span><em>did</em><span>, in fact, have an economic crash as a result of its real estate bust. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first way to see this is to look at China’s job market. In 2023, China </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d179406c-fa4b-4b49-beb6-ab826625852c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">famously modified</a><span> its youth unemployment data to use a narrow definition of unemployment, because the numbers were getting too high. In her tweet above, Kathleen Tyson declares that China “was the first to deflate a massive, leveraged housing bubble without a single quarter of economic contraction or loss of growth momentum in the real economy”. But is that true?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Well, no, it’s not. So by the kind of measurement Americans are used to hearing about, China’s economy officially contracted at an annualized rate of over -3% in the second quarter of 2022. This was also revised down from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a55061f3-898f-45f6-96e4-5025b2f54f69?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the -9.3% that was reported</a><span> in the initial version of the statistics. As for “loss of growth momentum”, China’s economy is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9a8377be-b03d-4e2c-9b2a-c932472402f2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">officially growing around 2 percentage points slower</a><span> than it was just before the pandemic. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So even if we accept the official numbers, the claim is wrong. But should we accept the official numbers? Probably not. There is evidence that the Chinese government “smooths” its growth numbers — in good years, it fudges downward, and in bad years it fudges upward. This is from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d6fcc9f6-1ce5-4e64-9fed-5a1ce941a8c5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Nakamura et al. (2016)</a><span>, who use detailed data on Chinese consumption to estimate how incomes changed:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Our estimates suggest that official statistics present a smoothed version of reality. We find that inflation was overestimated and growth underestimated by several percentage points per year in the late 1990s. In contrast, since 2002, official inflation statistics have risen only modestly, but our Engel curve based estimates have risen much more. Our estimates imply that growth was substantially lower than official statistics suggest since 2002, and actually dipped into negative territory in 2007 and 2008.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A bunch of analyses claim that China has also done this in response to the property crash. The Rhodium Group used alternative data sources </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0cc2bff4-b2ca-4bd0-9c3f-946ec7519d24?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">to estimate</a><span> that China’s economy actually shrank in 2022 and grew much more slowly in 2023 than the official numbers suggest:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Officially, China reported 3.0 percent real GDP growth in 2022, despite the fact that significant proportions of the economy were under strict lockdowns to prevent the spread of COVID-19 during large portions of the year, retail sales fell outright, and investment in the property sector was collapsing. In 2023, the decline in property investment continued, net exports and government spending were drags on growth, and household consumption growth remained relatively low. Beijing provided little direct assistance to households to facilitate spending, and Chinese households added to savings and paid down mortgage debt instead of spending more. Yet China officially reported 5.2 percent real GDP growth in 2023, barely slowing from the pre-pandemic pace of 6 percent in 2019, even though the property sector was experiencing a boom in 2019 and was collapsing in 2023…We estimate that real GDP growth was </span><strong><span>closer to a contraction of -0.3 percent to -0.8 percent in 2022, and there was only modest growth of 1.5 percent to 2 percent in 2023</span></strong><span>. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Bank of Finland was a little less negative, but still estimated that slowing economy. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It should be noted that there are a few analysts who disagree, and think that China’s growth numbers are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/31621bb7-cc29-49fb-81b2-677badd96ea4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">basically accurate</a><span>. But most independent assessments conclude that China’s growth not only suffered a sharp hit in 2022, but has been weaker in the years since the end of the pandemic. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It makes sense that China’s government would continue their traditional approach of smoothing out growth numbers in the short term in order to project an attitude of stability and calm. But smoothing only works if the economy eventually bounces back. If China is on a new longer-term trajectory of lower growth — which of course remains to be seen — then there will be too few good years to “pay back” the growth that was “borrowed” in the bad years of 2022 and beyond. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t want to detract from China’s accomplishment here, or say that its macroeconomic stability is entirely fake. China has invented — or, perhaps, perfected — an alternative tool for macroeconomic stabilization. Countries all over the world, including the United States, should study China’s financial stabilization policy and think about how to accomplish something similar without direct government control over bank management. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But at the same time, I don’t think we ought to be idolizing Chinese macroeconomic policy either. Even if there don’t turn out to be long-term productivity costs — which is a big “if” — China still hasn’t managed to rewrite the rules of aggregate demand and aggregate supply. </p><div 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>Today’s primer is a long, dense, wonkish discussion of an issue I’ve been steadily working on in the background. To be honest, this post is aimed primarily at economists, not a general audience. And I may well get professional pushback — in fact I hope I will. Anyway, apologies in advance for its relative inaccessibility, which I don’t intend to make a habit.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Europe is an economic superpower </span><span>that has </span><span>given its residents extraordinarily good lives both by historical standards and compared with the rest of the world. Yes, Europeans have smaller houses and cars than Americans do. Many of them also, as everyone has lately become aware, lack air conditioning. But they have much more economic security than most Americans, </span><span>lower economic inequality, longer </span><span>life expectancy, and more leisure time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There is, however, a widespread perception that Europe is living off its past glories, that it is lagging</span><span> behind</span><span> America and China in ways that will undermine its ability to maintain its </span><span>economic standing </span><span>in the world. This perception rests in part on the undeniable fact that Europe is home to few of the biggest technology companies and is almost completely shut out of the AI boom. It also reflects widely cited statistics: The most commonly discussed measures of growth in productivity and GDP point to an ever-growing gap between Europe and America.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But a funny thing happened on the way to inexorable European decline: If one compares </span><span>either </span><span>European GDP per capita or</span><span> European </span><span>productivity </span><span>(GDP per hour) </span><span>with that of the US</span><span> on a</span><span> year by year</span><span> basis</span><span>,</span><span> </span><span>using completely standard methods, one does </span><em>not</em><span> find an ever-growing gap. In fact, the gap between Europe and America has, if anything, narrowed somewhat over the past 25 years.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Understanding Europe’s economic performance is of huge importance, not just for Europeans, but for the rest of the world. The stakes go beyond economics. With authoritarianism on the rise in America, Europe is now the world’s great bastion of democracy. Hence it is important that it maintain its standing as a counterbalance to the US and China. Furthermore, Europe’s economic performance relative to the U.S. is often cited as a data point in debates on economic and social policy. Thus it’s important to understand what that record actually shows.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Finally, wearing my professional economist hat, what I call the US-EU paradox is </span><em>interesting</em><span>. </span><span>W</span><span>e have two ways of comparing major economies</span><span>:</span><span> one based on measured economic growth, one based on measured purchasing power. Both comparisons involve orthodox, widely accepted procedures. Both are carried out by eminently respectable statisticians and agencies. Yet they lead to starkly different conclusions. One says that Europe is in relative decline, while the other says it isn’t.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was first alerted to this strange dissonance in a February 2026 post by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f6812733-1256-4bf5-9f26-40485ecf5adf?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Seth Ackerman</a><span>. Since then I’ve been trying to make sense of the apparent contradiction.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today’s post is a detour </span><span>from my ongoing series on the implications of AI</span><span>, which I plan to return to next week. Here I will </span><span>offer a wonkish progress report on my</span><span> recent</span><span> efforts</span><span> to unpack the US-EU paradox</span><span>. </span><span>I will </span><span>argue that the preponderance of the evidence supports the view that Europe is </span><em>not</em><span> in relative decline. </span><span>I will show that comparisons</span><span> that seem to show Europe lagging </span><span>ignore important qualifications – qualifications that can render those comparisons misleading. First, there is a big difference between the EU and the US in industrial mix: the U.S. economy is more highly concentrated than Europe in “tech”, which creates a divergence in measured growth but not in living standards. Second, it is inherently difficult to measure growth in the face of technological change – a problem that doesn’t arise, notably, when comparing economies at a given point in time.</span></p><p
